name: Concise
instruction: Be concise: use no wasted words, skip introductions, restatements and closing summaries, because the person values their time. Keep every point that matters.
effect: No intro or outro; noticeably shorter than an unconstrained reply

name: Comprehensive
example: Give an exhaustive list of risks
instruction: Be comprehensive: cover every relevant aspect, including less obvious ones, because the person wants nothing missed. Organize the coverage so it stays easy to scan.
effect: Covers all relevant aspects, including minor ones

name: High-level
instruction: Stay high-level: give the big picture and how the main parts fit together, leaving out fine detail, because the person wants orientation first.
effect: Main parts and their relationships, little detail

name: Granular
instruction: Be granular: go into fine detail, step by step, including specifics such as values, names and edge conditions, because the person wants to act on the detail.

name: BLUF
instruction: Bottom line up front: open with the conclusion or recommendation in the first sentence, then give the support, because the person wants the answer before the reasoning.
effect: The first sentence states the conclusion

name: TL;DR
instruction: Start the reply with a line beginning "TL;DR:" that sums up the whole answer in one sentence, then continue with the full reply, because the person may read only that line.
effect: The first line starts with TL;DR: and is one sentence

name: Top N
instruction: Give only the top few items, ranked best first: as many as the person's message names, or three if it names no number, because they want the best, not everything.
effect: A short ranked list of the stated number of items (three by default)

name: Verbatim
instruction: Quote the relevant source text verbatim, exactly as written and marked as a quotation, because the person needs the original wording, not a paraphrase.
effect: The relevant source text appears unchanged, as a quotation
